title: How Coral Reefs Work
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain how coral reefs work: coral polyps as tiny carnivorous animals, their symbiosis with zooxanthellae algae, limestone (calcium carbonate) buildup, asexual and sexual reproduction, growth rates and conditions, coral sand and coralline algae, the three reef types (fringing, barrier, atoll) and reef zones (back, crest, fore reef, buttress zone), the Great Barrier Reef, threats such as bleaching, blast and cyanide fishing, runoff, mining and overfishing, economic value of reefs, and ways listeners can help. The episode also includes a South by Southwest live podcast announcement and a listener mail about a library in Malawi.

segments.title: Opening banter and coral reef introduction
segments.summary: Hosts trade health and vitamin chatter, Josh mentions his scuba certification at Cozumel, and they introduce the coral reef topic and the article by Jennifer Horton.

segments.title: Coral polyps and symbiosis with algae
segments.summary: Coral polyps are tiny living carnivorous animals, not plants, with stinging cells and sessile habits. They host zooxanthellae algae in a mutually beneficial symbiotic relationship in which the algae photosynthesize and share energy.

segments.title: How coral builds reefs and reproduces
segments.summary: Polyps use energy from the algae to secrete calcium carbonate limestone shelters. Colonies connect through tissue called coenosarc and their limestone joins into reefs. Corals grow by asexual cloning and by sexual reproduction, and growth is slow, about three inches a year under ideal conditions.

segments.title: Ideal conditions for coral growth
segments.summary: Reefs need equatorial warm waters, sunlight, clear water and low nutrients, with temperatures roughly 73 to 82 degrees Fahrenheit. Nutrient-rich, murky water hurts coral. Reefs are called old growth forests of the sea because they take thousands of years to form. Lifespan of individual coral is discussed but left unclear.
topics: old growth forests of the sea

segments.title: Coral sand and coralline algae
segments.summary: Broken coral pieces become coral sand, which coralline algae cement into gaps, repairing the reef. Coral sand mining is a threat because it removes this natural repair material.

segments.title: Types of reefs and reef zones
segments.summary: Three reef types are fringing, barrier and atoll, with an atoll forming from a sunken volcano ringed by reef. Reef zones are the back, crest, and fore reef, including the buttress zone, which funnels waves and shelters fish.

segments.title: Great Barrier Reef and largest living structures
segments.summary: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest living structure, visible from space, about 1,429 miles in a single reef system and roughly 18,500 miles of total edge. It hosts many coral and fish species and was protected as a national marine park and World Heritage Site. A comparison is made to a large Oregon fungus.

segments.title: Threats to coral reefs
segments.summary: Threats include coral bleaching from temperature rises of about one degree, El Nino weather, hurricanes, predators, blast fishing and cyanide fishing, overfishing, and runoff and sewage that increase nutrients. Only about five percent of reefs are in good condition, and about ten percent are beyond recovery.

segments.title: How to help and economic value of reefs
segments.summary: Listeners can adopt a reef, lobby for stricter fishing oversight, boycott products from blast-fishing countries, and avoid taking coral. Reefs are economically valuable, with Florida reefs worth about 8.5 billion dollars and worldwide tourism around 9.6 billion dollars annually.

segments.title: Listener mail from Malawi library
segments.summary: Listener Diane Bowls, a volunteer in Malawi, describes building a village library that uses podcasts and documentaries to help illiterate villagers learn.
